The sinking of the Titanic is one of the most infamous shipwrecks in history. On April 15, 1912, during her maiden voyage, the widely considered “unsinkable” RMS Titanic sank after colliding with an iceberg, resulting in the death of 1,502 out of 2,224 passengers and crew.

In this project, based on the classic Kaggle Titanic: Machine Learning from Disaster competition, we build an end-to-end classification pipeline using R, Tidyverse, and Tidymodels to predict which passengers survived the tragedy.

1. Environment & Setup

We begin by loading the core packages: tidyverse for data manipulation and tidymodels for a clean, unified modeling workflow.

# Load libraries
library(tidymodels)
library(tidyverse)

Next, we load the training and test datasets:

# Import datasets
titanic_train <- read_csv("train.csv")
titanic_test  <- read_csv("test.csv")

Let’s inspect the dimensions and structure of the datasets:

  • Train set: 891 rows, 12 columns
  • Test set: 418 rows, 11 columns (without the target variable Survived)

2. Exploratory Data Analysis & Missing Values

Before feature engineering, let’s combine both datasets to inspect missing values across the entire passenger population.

titanic_full <- bind_rows(titanic_train, titanic_test)

titanic_full |> 
  summarise_all(~ sum(is.na(.)))
# A tibble: 1 × 12
  PassengerId Survived Pclass  Name   Sex   Age SibSp Parch Ticket  Fare Cabin Embarked
        <int>    <int>  <int> <int> <int> <int> <int> <int>  <int> <int> <int>    <int>
            0      418      0     0     0   263     0     0      0     1  1014        2

Key Observations:

  • Survived: 418 missing values correspond precisely to the test dataset.
  • Age: 263 passengers have missing ages. We will impute this using K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN).
  • Cabin: Over 1,000 values are missing (nearly 77% of total records), so we drop this column to avoid sparse noise.
  • Embarked: Only 2 missing values, ideal for mode imputation.
  • Fare: Exactly 1 missing value in the test set, suitable for linear imputation.

3. Feature Engineering

Domain knowledge plays a crucial role in improving model accuracy. Here, we engineer two key features:

A. Family Size (FamilySize)

We combine SibSp (siblings / spouses aboard) and Parch (parents / children aboard) plus the passenger themselves (+1) to represent the total family size:

\[\text{FamilySize} = \text{SibSp} + \text{Parch} + 1\]

B. Title Extraction from Name

Passenger names contain social titles (Mr., Mrs., Miss., Master., Dr., Rev., etc.) that provide strong signals regarding age, gender, and social status.

# 1. Engineer FamilySize
titanic_full <- titanic_full |>
  mutate(FamilySize = SibSp + Parch + 1) |>
  select(-SibSp, -Parch)

# 2. Extract passenger title
titanic_full$title <- titanic_full$Name |>
  str_extract("([A-z]+)\\.") |>
  str_sub(end = -2)

# Check distribution of titles
titanic_full |>
  group_by(title) |>
  count() |>
  arrange(desc(n)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n))
# A tibble: 18 × 3
   title       n    prop
   <chr>   <int>   <dbl>
 1 Mr        757 0.578  
 2 Miss      260 0.199  
 3 Mrs       197 0.150  
 4 Master     61 0.0466 
 5 Rev         8 0.00611
 6 Dr          8 0.00611
 7 Col         4 0.00306
 8 Mlle        2 0.00153
 9 Major       2 0.00153
10 Ms          2 0.00153
# ℹ 8 more rows

Finally, we drop uninformative columns and convert categorical variables into factors:

titanic_full <- titanic_full |> 
  select(-Cabin, -Ticket, -Name) |> 
  mutate(across(c(Survived, Pclass, Sex, Embarked, title), as.factor))

4. Missing Data Imputation with Recipes

Instead of simple mean imputation, we use Tidymodels recipes to perform context-aware imputations: 1. Embarked: Mode imputation (step_impute_mode). 2. Fare: Linear regression imputation based on predictors (step_impute_linear). 3. Age: K-Nearest Neighbors imputation (step_impute_knn) using similar passenger profiles.

# Define imputation recipe
impute_recipe <- recipe(Survived ~ ., data = titanic_full) |>
  step_impute_mode(Embarked) |>
  step_impute_linear(Fare) |>
  step_impute_knn(Age) |>
  prep()

# Apply imputation
imputed <- bake(impute_recipe, new_data = titanic_full)

Age Group Discretization

To help tree-based models capture non-linear life-stage dynamics (e.g., children prioritized during lifeboat evacuation):

imputed <- imputed |> 
  mutate(Age = case_when(
    Age < 8 ~ "child",
    Age >= 8 & Age < 19 ~ "teenager",
    Age >= 19 & Age <= 60 ~ "adult",
    TRUE ~ "senior"
  )) |> 
  mutate(Age = as.factor(Age))

5. Modeling Workflow with Tidymodels

We split the processed data back into training (891 rows) and test (418 rows) sets, followed by an 80/20 train-validation split stratified by Survived.

titanic_train <- imputed |> slice(1:891)
titanic_test  <- imputed |> slice(892:1309)

set.seed(777)
split <- initial_split(titanic_train, prop = 0.8, strata = Survived)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)

Preprocessing Recipe & Cross-Validation

We normalize numeric predictors, collapse infrequent titles (threshold = 0.02), and create dummy variables for nominal features. We also set up 10-Fold Cross-Validation:

titanic_recipe <- recipe(Survived ~ ., data = train) |> 
  update_role(PassengerId, new_role = "id") |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_other(title, threshold = 0.02) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())

set.seed(345)
folds <- vfold_cv(train, v = 10, repeats = 1, strata = Survived)

6. Model Specification & Hyperparameter Tuning

We choose a Random Forest classifier using the high-performance ranger engine. We tune two critical hyperparameters: - mtry: Number of predictors sampled at each split. - min_n: Minimum number of data points in a node required for further splitting.

# Random Forest model specification
rf_spec <- rand_forest(
  mtry  = tune(),
  min_n = tune(),
  trees = 1000
) |> 
  set_engine("ranger") |>
  set_mode("classification")

# Combine recipe and model into a workflow
titanic_workflow <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(titanic_recipe) |>
  add_model(rf_spec)

# Tune hyperparameters across 10-fold cross validation
rf_tune <- tune_grid(
  titanic_workflow,
  resamples = folds,
  grid = 10, 
  control = control_grid(save_pred = TRUE, parallel_over = "everything")
)

7. Model Evaluation

Let’s examine the top-performing hyperparameter configurations based on classification accuracy:

show_best(rf_tune, metric = "accuracy")
# A tibble: 5 × 8
   mtry min_n .metric  .estimator  mean     n std_err .config              
  <int> <int> <chr>    <chr>      <dbl> <int>   <dbl> <chr>                
1     6    13 accuracy binary     0.844    10  0.0165 Preprocessor1_Model04
2     6    37 accuracy binary     0.838    10  0.0162 Preprocessor1_Model08
3    13    35 accuracy binary     0.837    10  0.0162 Preprocessor1_Model09
4     8    25 accuracy binary     0.836    10  0.0164 Preprocessor1_Model07
5     9    25 accuracy binary     0.834    10  0.0159 Preprocessor1_Model02

The best configuration achieves 84.4% cross-validated accuracy with mtry = 6 and min_n = 13.

Final Fit on Holdout Test Split

We finalize the workflow with the best hyperparameter configuration and evaluate on our held-out 20% validation split:

final_rf <- titanic_workflow |>
  finalize_workflow(select_best(rf_tune, metric = "accuracy"))

final_fit <- final_rf |>
  last_fit(split)

collect_metrics(final_fit)
# A tibble: 3 × 4
  .metric     .estimator .estimate .config             
  <chr>       <chr>          <dbl> <chr>               
1 accuracy    binary         0.849 Preprocessor1_Model1
2 roc_auc     binary         0.884 Preprocessor1_Model1
3 brier_class binary         0.116 Preprocessor1_Model1

Results Summary: - Test Accuracy: 84.9% - ROC-AUC: 0.884 - Brier Score: 0.116 (indicating well-calibrated probability predictions)

8. Generating Final Test Predictions

With our trained model, we generate survival predictions for Kaggle’s test dataset (test.csv):

final_model <- extract_workflow(final_fit)

predictions <- final_model |> 
  predict(titanic_test)

submission <- titanic_test |>
  select(PassengerId) |>
  bind_cols(predictions) |>
  rename(Survived = .pred_class)

# Export submission file
write_csv(submission, file = "predict.csv")
head(submission, 10)
# A tibble: 10 × 2
   PassengerId Survived
         <dbl> <fct>   
 1         892 0       
 2         893 1       
 3         894 0       
 4         895 0       
 5         896 1       
 6         897 0       
 7         898 1       
 8         899 0       
 9         900 1       
10         901 0

9. Conclusion & Takeaways

By leveraging Tidymodels, we maintained a clean, reproducible, and modular machine learning pipeline:

  1. Feature Engineering Impact: Deriving social titles (title) and family scale (FamilySize) provided strong predictive power beyond raw tabular columns.
  2. KNN Imputation: Replaced arbitrary age guessing with neighbor-based statistical imputation.
  3. Cross-Validation Tuning: Systematically optimized Random Forest hyperparameters, yielding a solid 84.9% accuracy and 0.884 ROC-AUC.

Feel free to explore the full repository on GitHub: nusaseldi/kaggle-datasets.

## 4. Missing Data Imputation with Recipes

Instead of simple mean imputation, we use Tidymodels `recipes` to perform context-aware imputations: 1. **`Embarked`**: Mode imputation (`step_impute_mode`). 2. **`Fare`**: Linear regression imputation based on predictors (`step_impute_linear`). 3. **`Age`**: K-Nearest Neighbors imputation (`step_impute_knn`) using similar passenger profiles.

``` r
# Define imputation recipe
impute_recipe <- recipe(Survived ~ ., data = titanic_full) |>
  step_impute_mode(Embarked) |>
  step_impute_linear(Fare) |>
  step_impute_knn(Age) |>
  prep()

# Apply imputation
imputed <- bake(impute_recipe, new_data = titanic_full)
```

### Age Group Discretization

To help tree-based models capture non-linear life-stage dynamics (e.g., children prioritized during lifeboat evacuation):

``` r
imputed <- imputed |> 
  mutate(Age = case_when(
    Age < 8 ~ "child",
    Age >= 8 & Age < 19 ~ "teenager",
    Age >= 19 & Age <= 60 ~ "adult",
    TRUE ~ "senior"
  )) |> 
  mutate(Age = as.factor(Age))
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 5. Modeling Workflow with Tidymodels

We split the processed data back into training (891 rows) and test (418 rows) sets, followed by an **80/20 train-validation split** stratified by `Survived`.

``` r
titanic_train <- imputed |> slice(1:891)
titanic_test  <- imputed |> slice(892:1309)

set.seed(777)
split <- initial_split(titanic_train, prop = 0.8, strata = Survived)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)
```

### Preprocessing Recipe & Cross-Validation

We normalize numeric predictors, collapse infrequent titles (`threshold = 0.02`), and create dummy variables for nominal features. We also set up **10-Fold Cross-Validation**:

``` r
titanic_recipe <- recipe(Survived ~ ., data = train) |> 
  update_role(PassengerId, new_role = "id") |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_other(title, threshold = 0.02) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())

set.seed(345)
folds <- vfold_cv(train, v = 10, repeats = 1, strata = Survived)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 6. Model Specification & Hyperparameter Tuning

We choose a **Random Forest** classifier using the high-performance `ranger` engine. We tune two critical hyperparameters: - `mtry`: Number of predictors sampled at each split. - `min_n`: Minimum number of data points in a node required for further splitting.

``` r
# Random Forest model specification
rf_spec <- rand_forest(
  mtry  = tune(),
  min_n = tune(),
  trees = 1000
) |> 
  set_engine("ranger") |>
  set_mode("classification")

# Combine recipe and model into a workflow
titanic_workflow <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(titanic_recipe) |>
  add_model(rf_spec)

# Tune hyperparameters across 10-fold cross validation
rf_tune <- tune_grid(
  titanic_workflow,
  resamples = folds,
  grid = 10, 
  control = control_grid(save_pred = TRUE, parallel_over = "everything")
)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 7. Model Evaluation

Let's examine the top-performing hyperparameter configurations based on classification accuracy:

``` r
show_best(rf_tune, metric = "accuracy")
```

```         
# A tibble: 5 × 8
   mtry min_n .metric  .estimator  mean     n std_err .config              
  <int> <int> <chr>    <chr>      <dbl> <int>   <dbl> <chr>                
1     6    13 accuracy binary     0.844    10  0.0165 Preprocessor1_Model04
2     6    37 accuracy binary     0.838    10  0.0162 Preprocessor1_Model08
3    13    35 accuracy binary     0.837    10  0.0162 Preprocessor1_Model09
4     8    25 accuracy binary     0.836    10  0.0164 Preprocessor1_Model07
5     9    25 accuracy binary     0.834    10  0.0159 Preprocessor1_Model02
```

The best configuration achieves **84.4% cross-validated accuracy** with `mtry = 6` and `min_n = 13`.

### Final Fit on Holdout Test Split

We finalize the workflow with the best hyperparameter configuration and evaluate on our held-out 20% validation split:

``` r
final_rf <- titanic_workflow |>
  finalize_workflow(select_best(rf_tune, metric = "accuracy"))

final_fit <- final_rf |>
  last_fit(split)

collect_metrics(final_fit)
```

```         
# A tibble: 3 × 4
  .metric     .estimator .estimate .config             
  <chr>       <chr>          <dbl> <chr>               
1 accuracy    binary         0.849 Preprocessor1_Model1
2 roc_auc     binary         0.884 Preprocessor1_Model1
3 brier_class binary         0.116 Preprocessor1_Model1
```

> **Results Summary:** - **Test Accuracy:** **84.9%** - **ROC-AUC:** **0.884** - **Brier Score:** **0.116** (indicating well-calibrated probability predictions)

## 8. Generating Final Test Predictions

With our trained model, we generate survival predictions for Kaggle's test dataset (`test.csv`):

``` r
final_model <- extract_workflow(final_fit)

predictions <- final_model |> 
  predict(titanic_test)

submission <- titanic_test |>
  select(PassengerId) |>
  bind_cols(predictions) |>
  rename(Survived = .pred_class)

# Export submission file
write_csv(submission, file = "predict.csv")
```

## 9. Conclusion & Takeaways

By leveraging **Tidymodels**, we maintained a clean, reproducible, and modular machine learning pipeline:

1.  **Feature Engineering Impact**: Deriving social titles (`title`) and family scale (`FamilySize`) provided strong predictive power beyond raw tabular columns.
2.  **KNN Imputation**: Replaced arbitrary age guessing with neighbor-based statistical imputation.
3.  **Cross-Validation Tuning**: Systematically optimized Random Forest hyperparameters, yielding a solid **84.9% accuracy** and **0.884 ROC-AUC**.
